title: Fine-grained MoE, shared experts, aux-loss-free load balancing
summary: How DeepSeekMoE and DeepSeek-V3 route tokens: many small experts, always-on shared experts, and a per-expert bias that balances load without an auxiliary loss.
outcomes: Explain how an MoE layer separates total parameters from per-token compute, and compute both for a real config
Explain why splitting experts into mN smaller ones and activating mK keeps FLOPs fixed but adds flexibility
Explain what shared experts are for and how they change the routed top-K
Compute the auxiliary balance loss for a small batch and explain its interference gradients
Trace the bias update of aux-loss-free balancing and DeepSeek-V3's group-limited gate step by step

lessons.title: From one MLP to many routed experts

blocks.md: In the GPT you built, every block has an attention layer followed by an MLP (also called the feed-forward network, FFN), and every token goes through all of the MLP's weights. That couples two things you might want to separate: the number of parameters (how much the model can store) and the compute spent per token. Make the MLP 4 times wider and every token pays 4 times the MLP FLOPs.

A **Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) layer** (Shazeer et al., 2017) breaks that coupling. It replaces one MLP with $N$ **experts**, each an ordinary MLP with its own weights, plus a small **router** (or gate) that looks at each token and picks only $K$ of the experts to run. Parameters grow with $N$; compute per token grows only with $K$. Switch Transformer uses $K=1$, GShard uses $K=2$.

The router is just a learned vector per expert, called the expert's **centroid** $e_i$. For the token's hidden state $u_t$, it computes an **affinity** score $s_{i,t}$ for every expert (a softmax over the dot products $u_t^\top e_i$), keeps the $K$ largest, and uses them as **gate values** $g_{i,t}$ that weight each chosen expert's output. Experts that are not chosen get gate 0 and are never computed.

blocks.tex: h_t = u_t + \sum_{i=1}^{N} g_{i,t}\,\mathrm{FFN}_i(u_t),\qquad g_{i,t} = \begin{cases} s_{i,t} & s_{i,t} \in \mathrm{Topk}(\{s_{j,t}\}, K) \\ 0 & \text{otherwise}\end{cases},\qquad s_{i,t} = \mathrm{Softmax}_i(u_t^\top e_i)
blocks.caption: The conventional MoE layer as written in the DeepSeekMoE paper (layer norm omitted). The residual $u_t$ is added back as in any Transformer block.

blocks.title: Router affinities for 4 tokens and 4 experts, top-2

scenes.caption: Each row is one token's softmax over the 4 experts, so each row sums to 1. These are toy numbers computed from made-up logits; a real router produces them from $u_t^\top e_i$.
Token t1 keeps its two largest scores: E1 (0.61) and E3 (0.22). Its MoE output is $u + 0.61\,\mathrm{FFN}_1(u) + 0.22\,\mathrm{FFN}_3(u)$. E2 and E4 are never run for this token.
Every token picks its own pair: t2 uses E2 and E4, t3 uses E1 and E2, t4 uses E3 and E4. Only half of the expert weights run for each token.

Count the picks per column: each expert received exactly 2 of the 8 token slots. This batch happens to be perfectly balanced. Nothing in the routing rule guarantees that, which is the problem of lessons 4 and 5.

blocks.title: One MoE layer: route, run K experts, combine

scenes.caption: The MoE layer sits where the MLP used to be. The router scores all experts, but only the chosen ones do any matrix multiplies.
Token t1: the router picks E1 and E3. Their outputs are scaled by the gate values 0.61 and 0.22 and summed with the residual.
Token t4 takes a different path through the same layer: E3 (0.72) and E4 (0.12). Different tokens use different parameters, which is how total parameters exceed per-token compute.

blocks.md: Separate two numbers for every MoE model: **total parameters** (all experts, what you store) and **activated parameters** (what one token actually uses, which sets FLOPs per token). DeepSeek-V3 has 671B total and 37B activated per token.

This course is about three refinements DeepSeek-AI introduced on top of this layer: **fine-grained experts** (many small experts instead of a few big ones), **shared experts** (a few experts that every token uses), and **auxiliary-loss-free load balancing** (keeping experts evenly used without adding a balancing term to the loss). DeepSeek-V3 combines all three.

blocks.question: An MoE layer has 16 experts, each the same size as the dense MLP it replaced, with top-2 routing. Compared with the dense MLP, what happens to parameters and per-token FLOPs in that layer?
options: Both grow 16 times
Parameters grow 2 times; FLOPs grow 16 times
Parameters grow 16 times; per-token FLOPs grow about 2 times, plus a tiny router cost
Parameters grow 16 times; per-token FLOPs stay exactly the same as dense
blocks.explain: Every expert is stored, so parameters scale with N = 16. Each token runs only K = 2 experts, so expert FLOPs are 2 times the dense MLP. The router (one dot product per expert) adds a little on top. With top-1 routing (Switch), expert FLOPs would match the dense MLP.

blocks.prompt: In the figure, all four experts got exactly 2 token slots. Will a learned router keep load balanced like this on its own as training goes on?
blocks.reveal: Not reliably. Shazeer et al. (2017) observed that the gating network tends to converge to always giving large weights to the same few experts, and that this is self-reinforcing: favored experts train faster, so they get picked even more. This is **routing collapse**, and every method in lessons 4 to 6 exists to prevent it.

lessons.title: Fine-grained experts: split each expert into m slices

blocks.md: Conventional MoE models use a small number of experts, for example 8 or 16. The DeepSeekMoE paper argues this causes **knowledge hybridity**: with so few experts, the tokens routed to any one expert cover many unrelated kinds of knowledge, so that expert must cram them all into one set of weights that are hard to use at the same time.

**Fine-grained expert segmentation** fixes this without changing the budget. Take each expert's MLP and cut its intermediate hidden dimension into $m$ slices, giving $mN$ experts that are each $1/m$ the size. To keep compute constant, activate $mK$ of them instead of $K$. Total expert parameters stay at $N$ standard MLPs, and per-token FLOPs stay at $K$ standard MLPs.

blocks.title: The same 16 hidden units, cut ever finer

scenes.caption: Conventional: 4 experts (N = 4), each 4 hidden units wide, top-1 routing (K = 1). One token can only use one fixed block of 4 units.
m = 2: 8 experts of 2 units each, top-2. Still 4 active units per token, same FLOPs, but the token can now take half of the old E1 and half of the old E4.
m = 4: 16 experts of 1 unit each, top-4. Same 16 parameters' worth of units, same 4 active per token, but any 4 of 16 can be combined. This is the mN choose mK flexibility the paper is after.

blocks.tex: h_t = u_t + \sum_{i=1}^{mN} g_{i,t}\,\mathrm{FFN}_i(u_t),\qquad g_{i,t} \neq 0 \ \text{only for}\ s_{i,t} \in \mathrm{Topk}(\{s_{j,t}\}_{j=1}^{mN},\ mK)
blocks.caption: Fine-grained MoE: same equation as before with $mN$ experts and $mK$ active. Each $\mathrm{FFN}_i$ now has $1/m$ of the original intermediate width.

blocks.md: The gain is in the number of distinct expert combinations a token can use. With $N = 16$ and top-2 there are $\binom{16}{2} = 120$ combinations. Split each expert in 4 ($m = 4$) and activate 8 of 64: $\binom{64}{8} = 4{,}426{,}165{,}368$. The parameter count and FLOPs did not change; only the menu got far richer.

blocks.title: Possible expert combinations per token (log10), N = 16, K = 2

scenes.caption: Conventional top-2 of 16 experts gives 120 combinations, about $10^{2.08}$.
Splitting each expert further keeps FLOPs fixed, yet the count of combinations explodes: m = 4 gives about 4.4 billion, and m = 8 about $10^{20}$.

blocks.md: Does it work? In the paper's 2B-parameter validation runs (100B training tokens, all MoE models with the same total parameters), the Pile test loss fell from 1.867 for GShard (top-2) to 1.808 for DeepSeekMoE with the same activated parameters. DeepSeekMoE here is fine-grained and also uses one shared expert, the topic of the next lesson. It matched a GShard model with 1.5 times the expert parameters and compute (also 1.808).

blocks.title: Pile test loss, 2B-scale MoE comparisons (lower is better)

scenes.caption: Dense is the 0.2B baseline. Hash Layer and Switch (top-1) have 0.2B active; GShard (top-2) and DeepSeekMoE have 0.3B active; all MoE models have 2.0B total. Numbers from DeepSeekMoE Table 1.
GShard x1.5 has 1.5 times the expert parameters and expert compute of GShard, yet only ties DeepSeekMoE at 1.808 (Table 2).

blocks.md: Finer is not free forever. Each expert becomes a smaller matrix multiply, which uses the GPU less efficiently. DeepSeekMoE 16B stopped at experts one quarter the size of a standard FFN, citing the potential loss of computational efficiency from excessively small experts. DeepSeek-V3 uses 256 routed experts with an intermediate width of 2048.

The paper's ablation (Figure 3) segmented each expert into 2 and then 4 pieces while holding total and activated parameters fixed, and saw overall benchmark performance improve with each step of finer granularity.

blocks.question: You split each of 16 experts into 4 (64 experts total) but forget to change top-2 routing. What happens?
options: Per-token expert compute drops to one quarter, because 2 small experts are only half of one original expert
Nothing changes; the layer has the same parameters and FLOPs
Per-token compute rises 4 times because there are 4 times as many experts
The router stops working because softmax needs exactly 16 outputs
blocks.explain: Segmentation keeps compute constant only if you also raise the number of active experts from K to mK, here from 2 to 8. With top-2 of 64 quarter-size experts, each token uses 2/4 = 0.5 of one original expert instead of 2, a quarter of the FLOPs. Total parameters are unchanged.

blocks.question: Why is the combinatorial count, not the expert count, the quantity the paper highlights?
options: Because more combinations means more FLOPs
Because routers need at least a billion options to converge
Because GPUs schedule experts by combination
Because each token's computation is a sum over its chosen experts, so more possible subsets means a more precisely targeted mix of knowledge at the same cost
blocks.explain: A token's MoE output is the gated sum of its chosen experts. With 120 possible pairs, many different kinds of tokens must share the same pair. With billions of possible 8-subsets of small experts, the token can assemble a closer fit. FLOPs are identical in both designs.

lessons.title: Shared experts: an always-on path for common knowledge

blocks.md: The second problem DeepSeekMoE names is **knowledge redundancy**. Tokens sent to different experts often still need the same common knowledge (basic syntax, frequent words). If every expert must learn it on its own, many experts store copies of the same thing and less capacity is left for specialization.

**Shared expert isolation** gives that common knowledge a home. Set aside $K_s$ experts as **shared experts** that every token passes through, with no router involved. To keep compute constant, the router now picks $mK - K_s$ routed experts instead of $mK$. The paper credits the prototype of this idea to Rajbhandari et al. (2022, DeepSpeed-MoE), who arrived at it from an engineering angle.

blocks.tex: h_t = u_t + \sum_{i=1}^{K_s} \mathrm{FFN}_i(u_t) + \sum_{i=K_s+1}^{mN} g_{i,t}\,\mathrm{FFN}_i(u_t),\qquad g_{i,t}\ \text{nonzero for the top}\ (mK - K_s)\ \text{routed experts}
blocks.caption: The full DeepSeekMoE layer. The first sum has no gate: shared experts always run with weight 1.

scenes.caption: The shared expert S has no router edge: every token goes through it. Routed experts R1 to R6 stand in for the many fine-grained experts.
A code token: S runs, and the router adds R1 and R4 for the specialized part.
A math token: S runs again, but the routed pair is now R2 and R6. Common knowledge lives in S once, so the routed experts do not each need a copy.

blocks.md: Evidence from the 2B experiments: with 1 shared expert and 7 of 63 routed experts active, the Pile loss was 1.808. Disabling the shared expert and activating one more routed expert instead (same compute) raised it to **2.414**. The routed experts cannot stand in for what the shared expert learned.

How many shared experts? Holding 64 total and the active count fixed, 1, 2 and 4 shared experts gave Pile losses of 1.808, 1.806 and 1.811, a small difference. The authors kept a ratio of 1 shared expert to 3 activated routed experts when scaling up.

Real configurations, from the papers and DeepSeek-V3's released config:

- **DeepSeekMoE 2B**: 1 shared + 63 routed experts, each 0.25 of a standard FFN; 1 + 7 active (2 FFNs' worth).
- **DeepSeekMoE 16B**: 2 shared + 64 routed, each 0.25 of a standard FFN; 2 + 6 active. 16.4B total, 2.8B activated, 74.4T vs 183.5T FLOPs per 4K tokens against dense DeepSeek 7B (40.5%).
- **DeepSeek-V3**: 1 shared + 256 routed, intermediate width 2048, 1 + 8 active, in 58 of its 61 layers (the first 3 stay dense).

A neat consistency check on V3: 9 active experts of width 2048 make $9 \times 2048 = 18432$ active hidden units, exactly the intermediate width (`inter_dim` 18432) of the 3 dense FFN layers. Per token, each MoE layer costs the same FLOPs as a dense one while storing 257 experts.

blocks.title: Where DeepSeek-V3's parameters live (billions, from config_671B.json)

scenes.caption: Total: each expert is a SwiGLU MLP with three weight matrices, $3 \times 7168 \times 2048 \approx 44.0$M weights. 58 layers x 256 routed experts is about 653.9B, 97% of the computed 671.0B total. Attention (MLA, V3's compressed attention) is 11.4B.

Activated per token: only 8 routed experts per layer run, about 20.4B, while shared experts, attention, embeddings and dense layers are always used. The bars sum to about 37.4B, or 37.6B with router weights, matching the report's 37B.

blocks.md: Simplified accounting: the bars leave out the 0.1B of router weights and small norm vectors (with them the computed total is 671.0B), and the count covers the 61 main layers only. The released config and the paper agree.

blocks.question: In the 2B ablation, removing the shared expert and activating one extra routed expert kept FLOPs equal but raised Pile loss from 1.808 to 2.414. What is the best reading?
options: The routed experts were undertrained, so any extra routed expert would hurt
The shared expert had learned common knowledge that the specialized routed experts do not hold, so it is not interchangeable with a routed one
Shared experts are larger than routed experts, so removing one removes compute
The loss rose because the router softmax had one fewer output
blocks.explain: Both configurations use the same number and size of active experts. The jump shows the shared expert holds something the routed experts never learned because they could rely on it: the common knowledge the design meant to isolate.

blocks.question: A team configures 2 shared + 64 routed quarter-size experts and routes to 8 routed experts, keeping the same 2 shared. Compared with DeepSeekMoE 16B (2 + 6 active), what changed?
options: Nothing; shared experts do not count toward compute
Total parameters rose by 2 experts
Activated expert compute rose from 8 to 10 quarter-experts, i.e. from 2 to 2.5 standard FFNs per token
Only the router cost changed
blocks.explain: Shared experts always run, so they count fully toward activated compute. DeepSeekMoE lowers the routed top-K by $K_s$ to keep compute fixed: 2 + 6 = 8 quarter-size experts = 2 FFNs. Using 2 + 8 means 10 quarters = 2.5 FFNs, 25% more expert FLOPs.

lessons.title: Load imbalance, routing collapse and the auxiliary loss

blocks.md: Load imbalance hurts in two ways. First, **routing collapse**: the router settles on a few favored experts, those train faster and get picked even more, and the rest are barely trained. Second, systems cost: with **expert parallelism** (different experts on different GPUs), the GPU holding the busiest expert sets the time of the whole step while others idle.

Switch Transformer makes the cost concrete. Its compiled kernels need static shapes, so each expert gets a fixed **expert capacity**: tokens per batch divided by number of experts, times a **capacity factor**. Tokens beyond capacity are **dropped**: the expert skips them and they pass to the next layer only through the residual connection. A larger factor drops fewer tokens but wastes compute and memory on padding.

blocks.title: Toy batch: 8 tokens, 4 experts, top-1 routing

scenes.caption: A collapsing router sends 5 of 8 tokens to E1 and none to E4. Perfect balance would be 2 each.
Capacity factor 1.0: capacity is 8 / 4 x 1.0 = 2 tokens. E1 drops 3 of its 5 tokens, so 3 of 8 tokens skip this layer's FFN entirely.
Capacity factor 1.5: capacity 3, E1 still drops 2 tokens. Factor 2.0 (capacity 4) drops 1. Buying slack fights the symptom while E4 sits idle.
Balanced routing: 2 tokens per expert. Nothing is dropped even at capacity factor 1.0 and every GPU does equal work.

blocks.md: The standard fix (Shazeer et al. 2017; GShard; Switch) is an **auxiliary balance loss** added to the language-modeling loss. In the form used by DeepSeekMoE and the loss-free paper, for $N$ experts, top-$K$ routing and $T$ tokens:

blocks.tex: \mathcal{L}_{\text{Bal}} = \alpha \sum_{i=1}^{N} f_i P_i,\qquad f_i = \frac{N}{K T} \sum_{t=1}^{T} \mathbb{1}(\text{token } t \text{ selects expert } i),\qquad P_i = \frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T} s_{i,t}
blocks.caption: $f_i$ is the expert's share of routed slots scaled so that perfect balance gives $f_i = 1$; $P_i$ is its average router score. $\alpha$ sets the strength.

blocks.md: Work the toy batch. Balanced: $f = (1, 1, 1, 1)$ and, with uniform scores, $P = (0.25, 0.25, 0.25, 0.25)$, so $\sum f_i P_i = 1.0$. Collapsed: counts $(5, 2, 1, 0)$ give $f = (2.5, 1, 0.5, 0)$; with average scores $P = (0.5, 0.25, 0.15, 0.10)$ the sum is $1.25 + 0.25 + 0.075 + 0 = 1.575$. The loss is larger when the experts that get the most tokens also get the most probability.

$f_i$ comes from a hard top-K count and has no gradient. The gradient flows through $P_i$: it pushes down the router scores of overloaded experts. The Switch paper notes the loss is minimized under uniform routing.

blocks.title: Balance loss for 2 experts, top-1, as routing skews

scenes.caption: Simplified: assume each expert's average score equals its share of tokens. Then $\sum f_i P_i = 2(x^2 + (1-x)^2)$, minimized at the even split x = 0.5 where the loss is exactly $\alpha$.
A smaller $\alpha$ flattens the whole curve: the push toward balance weakens, and so does the gradient it injects into the router. That knob is the whole dilemma.

blocks.md: **The dilemma.** The balance gradient competes with the language-modeling gradient. The loss-free paper (Wang et al., 2024) swept $\alpha$ over 1e-2, 1e-3, 1e-4 and 0: small $\alpha$ led to routing collapse, large $\alpha$ kept load balanced but notably worsened perplexity. Switch used $\alpha = 10^{-2}$; DeepSeekMoE used 0.01 at 2B and only 0.001 at 16B, noting that a larger factor did not improve efficiency in their setup but did hurt quality.

A balance loss is not a free regularizer. Its gradient changes the router toward balance, not toward predicting the next token. The loss-free paper calls these **interference gradients**, and they are the reason a strong $\alpha$ costs model quality.

DeepSeekMoE also added a **device-level** balance loss: group the experts by the device they live on and balance the groups instead of individual experts, with a small expert-level $\alpha_1$ (just enough to avoid collapse) and a larger device-level $\alpha_2$. Balancing what the hardware actually waits on, rather than every expert, constrains the router less.

blocks.question: 4 experts, top-1, 8 tokens. Counts are (4, 2, 2, 0) and average router scores are P = (0.4, 0.3, 0.2, 0.1). What is the sum of $f_i P_i$ (the loss divided by alpha)?
blocks.explain: $f_i = \frac{N}{KT} c_i = \frac{4}{8} c_i$, so f = (2, 1, 1, 0). Then 2(0.4) + 1(0.3) + 1(0.2) + 0(0.1) = 0.8 + 0.3 + 0.2 = 1.3, above the balanced value of 1.0. 0.325 is what you get if you forget the N/(KT) scaling and use raw fractions (0.5, 0.25, 0.25, 0).

blocks.question: Your MoE drops 4% of tokens at capacity factor 1.0. A teammate proposes raising the capacity factor to 2.0 and calling it fixed. What is the main cost?
options: None; capacity factor only affects inference
Each expert now reserves room for twice its fair share, so compute and memory are spent on padding while the underlying imbalance (and idle experts) remains
The auxiliary loss becomes undefined
Tokens are now routed to two experts each
blocks.explain: Capacity is a buffer per expert. Doubling it reduces drops but wastes compute and memory whenever experts are below capacity, which, under imbalance, is most of them. The Switch paper describes exactly this trade-off, and its Switch models performed better at low capacity factors (1.0 and 1.25).

lessons.title: Aux-loss-free balancing: steer the router with a bias

blocks.md: **Loss-Free Balancing** (Wang, Gao, Zhao, Sun and Dai, DeepSeek-AI, 2024) controls load without any balance loss. Each expert gets a scalar **bias** $b_i$. The bias is added to the affinity scores only when choosing the top-K experts. The gate values that weight the experts' outputs still use the original scores.

blocks.tex: g_{i,t} = \begin{cases} s_{i,t} & s_{i,t} + b_i \in \mathrm{Topk}(\{s_{j,t} + b_j\}_{j=1}^{N},\ K) \\ 0 & \text{otherwise}\end{cases}
blocks.caption: The bias decides who is selected; the unbiased score decides how much the selected expert contributes.

blocks.md: The biases are not learned by gradient descent. After each training step, count the tokens $c_i$ each expert received, compare with the mean $\bar c$, and move each bias by a fixed step $u$: up if the expert was underloaded, down if overloaded. That is Algorithm 1 of the paper, with update rule $b_i \leftarrow b_i + u \cdot \mathrm{sign}(\bar c - c_i)$.

blocks.title: Algorithm 1 on the toy batch
blocks.code:
u = 0.05                    # bias update rate (paper: 0.001)
b = zeros(n_experts)        # one bias per expert, starts at 0
for batch in data:
    s = router_scores(batch)            # [T, n_experts]
    pick = topk(s + b, k=2)             # bias steers selection only
    g = gather(s, pick)                 # gates use the raw scores
    loss = lm_loss(batch, pick, g)      # no balance term
    loss.backward(); opt.step()         # b gets no gradient
    c = bincount(pick, n_experts)       # tokens per expert
    e = c.mean() - c                    # > 0 means underloaded
    b = b + u * sign(e)                 # nudge toward balance

scenes.caption: All biases start at 0, so the first step routes exactly like a plain top-K router.

vars.picks: A appears in all 8 tokens' top-2

scenes.caption: Selection uses s + b. The gate values come from s itself, so the forward computation is the model's honest opinion of each chosen expert.
The training loss is only the language-modeling loss. Nothing in it mentions balance, so no interference gradient reaches the router.
After the step, count each expert's tokens. A and B are over the mean of 4; C and D are under.
Each bias moves by exactly u in the direction of its error's sign. The size of the error does not matter in this rule.
Step 1: B is now under the mean, so its bias swings back up to 0 while A keeps sinking.

blocks.title: Expert loads per step in the toy (8 tokens, top-2, u = 0.05)

scenes.caption: Step 0, all biases 0: routing follows raw scores. Expert A takes all 8 tokens, D gets 1. Mean load is 4 (8 tokens x top-2 / 4 experts). MaxVio = (8 - 4) / 4 = 1.0.
Biases after one update: A and B were above 4, so they drop by u = 0.05; C and D rise. Loads become (8, 3, 3, 2): B lost slots, A has not moved yet.
Step 2, bias (-0.10, 0, +0.10, +0.10): loads (7, 4, 3, 2), MaxVio 0.75. Overloaded experts keep sinking, underloaded ones keep rising.
Step 3, bias (-0.15, 0, +0.15, +0.15). A is down to 6. B's bias stalled at 0 because its load was exactly 4 last step: sign(0) = 0.
Step 4, bias (-0.20, +0.05, +0.15, +0.20): loads (6, 3, 4, 3), MaxVio 0.5. Overloaded experts keep sinking, underloaded ones keep rising.
Step 5, bias (-0.25, +0.10, +0.15, +0.25): loads (5, 4, 3, 4), MaxVio 0.25. No gradient was ever involved; only the four bias numbers moved.
Step 6, bias (-0.30, +0.10, +0.20, +0.25): loads (4, 3, 4, 5), MaxVio 0.25. Overloaded experts keep sinking, underloaded ones keep rising.
From here the toy oscillates between (4, 3, 4, 5) and (4, 5, 4, 3): 16 slots over 8 tokens are too coarse to hit 4 each every step. Real batches have millions of slots, and u is 0.001.

blocks.md: Simplified: in this toy the router scores are frozen, so only the bias moves. In real training the router weights also change each step, and the bias keeps tracking the load. The 8 token-by-4 expert scores and every load and bias shown were computed by a script.

Look at one token at step 6, bias $(-0.30, +0.10, +0.20, +0.25)$. Its raw scores are $(0.80, 0.70, 0.20, 0.35)$, so a plain router would pick A and B. Biased scores are $(0.50, 0.80, 0.40, 0.60)$, so it picks **B and D** instead. Its gates use the raw 0.70 and 0.35; normalized over the chosen pair as DeepSeek-V3 does, that is $0.67$ and $0.33$.

blocks.prompt: The toy used u = 0.05. Predict what happens with u = 0.1 (bigger steps).
blocks.reveal: It gets near balance faster (MaxVio 0.25 at step 3) but then overshoots: at step 4 loads jump to (2, 7, 4, 3), MaxVio 0.75, and it keeps swinging. The paper saw the same effect at scale: u = 0.0001 converged too slowly early in training, u = 0.01 caused fluctuations late in training, and u = 0.001 was best (validation perplexity 9.50 vs 9.51 for both others).

blocks.md: The bias changes **which** experts a token uses, never **how much** a chosen expert contributes, and it receives no gradient. That is how Loss-Free Balancing controls load without fighting the language-modeling objective.

Why update from the **previous** batch instead of balancing the current one exactly? Because using the current sequence's load would let later tokens influence earlier tokens' routing, leaking information about the future in a causal language model. **Expert Choice** routing, where each expert picks its top tokens, balances perfectly but has exactly this leak: the paper estimates a 9-layer model with 16 experts and 2 per token could leak about 50 bits per token, and observed an abnormal 10% loss drop when it made leakage easier.

**Results** (1B model on 100B tokens, 3B on 200B tokens, sigmoid gating, DeepSeekMoE backbone). The paper measures balance with **MaxVio** = $(\max_i \text{Load}_i - \overline{\text{Load}}) / \overline{\text{Load}}$, how far the busiest expert is above a perfectly even share. Against an auxiliary loss with $\alpha$ = 0.001:

blocks.title: Loss-controlled vs Loss-Free (Wang et al., Table 2)

scenes.caption: Global MaxVio on validation data, averaged over layers: the busiest expert was 72% (1B) and 52% (3B) over its fair share with the aux loss, but only 4% with Loss-Free Balancing.
Validation perplexity at the same time: 9.56 vs 9.50 at 1B and 7.97 vs 7.92 at 3B. Better balance and slightly better quality, no trade-off.

blocks.question: A colleague's implementation computes `weights = gather(s + b, pick)` and multiplies expert outputs by those weights. What is wrong?
options: Nothing; using the biased score everywhere is the method
The top-K must be taken on s alone, and the bias added after
The bias should be multiplied, not added
The bias now changes each expert's contribution to the output, so a balancing knob leaks into the model's function; gates must use the raw scores s
blocks.explain: The paper and DeepSeek-V3 both state that the bias is only used for routing; the gate value comes from the original affinity. With the bug, an underloaded expert's output is inflated just because it was underloaded, which distorts the forward pass. (A multiplicative bias was tested and was slightly worse, but it too only affects selection.)

blocks.question: Why does Algorithm 1 use sign(e) rather than e itself?
options: The paper tried b += u x e and found it slightly better balanced but no better in perplexity, so it kept the simpler sign rule
sign(e) is required for causality
Using e would make the bias receive gradients
sign(e) guarantees exact balance every step
blocks.explain: Table 3 of the paper compares variants: the proportional rule reached MaxVio 0.028 to 0.040 with perplexity 9.51 to 9.53, versus 0.044 and 9.50 for the sign rule with u = 0.001. Neither variant involves gradients or future tokens.

lessons.title: Putting it together: routing in DeepSeek-V3

blocks.md: DeepSeek-V3 (671B total, 37B activated) uses all three ideas. Each of its 58 MoE layers has 1 shared and 256 routed experts, picks 8 routed experts per token, and balances them with the bias method. Two details differ from DeepSeekMoE: affinities use a **sigmoid** per expert instead of a softmax across experts, and the chosen experts' scores are **normalized** to sum to 1 to give the gates.

blocks.tex: s_{i,t} = \sigma(u_t^\top e_i),\qquad g'_{i,t} = \begin{cases} s_{i,t} & s_{i,t} + b_i \in \mathrm{Topk}(\{s_{j,t} + b_j\}, K_r) \\ 0 & \text{otherwise}\end{cases},\qquad g_{i,t} = \frac{g'_{i,t}}{\sum_j g'_{j,t}}
blocks.caption: DeepSeek-V3 routing (Eqs. 13 to 16 of the report, with the bias). $K_r = 8$.

blocks.md: There is also a hardware constraint. Experts are spread over 64 GPUs in 8 nodes, and cross-node InfiniBand (50 GB/s) is about 3.2 times slower than in-node NVLink (160 GB/s). So V3 uses **node-limited routing**: each token may go to at most $M = 4$ nodes, chosen by the sum of the highest $K_r/M$ affinity scores of the experts on each node. The released inference code expresses the same idea as **group-limited** routing: 8 expert groups (`n_expert_groups`), keep the best 4 (`n_limited_groups`), scoring each group by the sum of its top-2 biased scores.

blocks.title: Group-limited gate on a toy token (8 experts, 4 groups)
blocks.code:
def gate(x, W, bias, n_groups=4, keep_groups=2, k=3, scale=2.5):
    s = sigmoid(x @ W.T)                     # affinity per expert
    biased = s + bias                        # bias only steers selection
    g = biased.view(n_groups, -1)            # 8 experts -> 4 groups of 2
    group_score = g.topk(2).values.sum(-1)   # sum of top-2 per group
    keep = group_score.topk(keep_groups).indices
    mask = ones(n_groups, dtype=bool); mask[keep] = False
    g = g.masked_fill(mask[:, None], -inf).flatten()
    idx = g.topk(k).indices                  # chosen experts
    w = s[idx]                               # raw scores, not biased
    w = w / w.sum()                          # normalize (sigmoid case)
    return w * scale, idx

scenes.caption: Sigmoid affinities for one token. Raw ranking: expert 5 (0.818), expert 0 (0.769), expert 3 (0.711). Simplified from DeepSeek-V3's inference/model.py Gate.forward, shrunk to 8 experts.
The load-balancing biases (set by the update rule, not by gradients) are added. Expert 5 has been overloaded (bias -0.15) and expert 4 underloaded (+0.20).
Experts are grouped in pairs; each group's score is the sum of its 2 best biased scores. Group 1 (experts 2, 3) leads.
Only the top 2 groups survive. Expert 0, the second-best raw score, is cut because its group lost. This is the price of capping communication.
Top-3 among eligible biased scores: experts 3 (0.761), 7 (0.690), 6 (0.575). Without groups the choice would have been 3, 0, 7.
Gates come from the unbiased scores, normalized to sum to 1, then multiplied by route_scale (2.5 in config_671B.json).
A token's chosen experts may sit on many nodes. Each cross-node hop uses slow InfiniBand, so the router first ranks nodes.
Nodes are scored from their experts' best affinities; only the top M survive (V3 uses M = 4 of 8 nodes). Experts on nodes B and D are now ineligible for this token.
The token crosses InfiniBand once per kept node, landing on the GPU with the same in-node index, then NVLink forwards it to the GPUs that host its experts.

blocks.md: Training settings from the report: bias update speed $\gamma = 0.001$ for the first 14.3T tokens, then $\gamma = 0$ (biases frozen) for the last 500B. A **complementary sequence-wise balance loss** with a tiny $\alpha = 0.0001$ guards against extreme imbalance inside any single sequence. Thanks to good balance, V3 drops no tokens in training; deployment strategies such as redundant experts keep inference drop-free too.

Why mostly batch-wise balancing? A sequence-wise loss forces each sequence to spread over all experts, even a sequence that is entirely code. Batch-wise balancing only asks the whole batch to be even, so experts can specialize by domain. The report shows clearer domain-specific expert load in an aux-loss-free 16B model, and at 1B scale validation loss was 2.258 with a sequence-wise loss vs 2.253 for both the loss-free method and a batch-wise aux loss (3B: 2.085 vs 2.080 and 2.080).

blocks.title: Aux-loss-based vs aux-loss-free at 228.7B total (DeepSeek-V3 Table 5)

scenes.caption: Baseline balanced purely with auxiliary losses (20.9B activated, 578B training tokens).
Same data and architecture, auxiliary losses removed, bias balancing added. Most benchmarks improve (HumanEval 46.3, GSM8K 74.5); MMLU slipped from 68.3 to 67.2. Gains are typical, not universal.

blocks.md: Serving adds its own balancing. Load observed online decides which experts are hot; V3 duplicates high-load experts (**redundant experts**), re-chosen periodically such as every 10 minutes, with 32 redundant experts in the prefill deployment. In decoding, the shared expert is treated as a routed expert that is always selected, so each token picks 9 experts, with 64 GPUs hosting redundant and shared experts.

Batch-level balance has two weak spots the report names: imbalance inside a single sequence or small batch, and **domain shift** at inference (a deployment flooded with one kind of input overloads that domain's experts). V3 answers the first with large training batches plus the tiny sequence-wise loss, and the second with redundant experts at serving time.

blocks.question: In the gate trace, expert 0 had the second-highest raw affinity (0.769) but was not chosen. Why?
options: Its bias was negative enough to drop it below experts 6 and 7
Sigmoid scores above 0.75 are clipped
Its group (experts 0 and 1) had a lower group score than groups 1 and 3, so the whole group was masked before the top-k
Shared experts always take the place of expert 0
blocks.explain: Group 0 scored 0.719 + 0.501 = 1.220, behind groups 1 (1.335) and 3 (1.265). Masking happens before the expert-level top-k, so expert 0's biased 0.719, which would beat expert 7's 0.690, never competes. That is the deliberate cost of limiting how many nodes a token touches.

blocks.question: DeepSeek-V3 relies on the bias method yet still keeps a sequence-wise balance loss with alpha = 0.0001. What is the best justification?
options: The bias method does not work without an auxiliary loss
The bias balances load across whole batches; the tiny loss only guards against extreme imbalance within a single sequence, while staying too weak to cause meaningful interference gradients
The loss replaces the bias during the final 500B tokens
It is needed to train the router weights at all
blocks.explain: The report calls it complementary: the main balancing is aux-loss-free, and the sequence-wise term exists just to avoid extreme per-sequence imbalance. Its alpha is ten times smaller than the 0.001 baseline used in the loss-free paper. Router weights are trained by the language-modeling loss through the gate values.

blocks.question: A team copies V3's recipe but trains with very small global batches (a few sequences per step). Which risk grows most?
options: Future-token leakage from the bias
The shared expert stops training
Node-limited routing stops working
Per-step load imbalance, since batch-wise balancing cannot even out a batch that is mostly one domain, so busy experts stall the step
blocks.explain: The loss-free paper shows balance improving as the computation batch grows, and the V3 report lists imbalance within small batches as a challenge that large-scale expert and data parallelism solves. The bias uses only past batches, so there is no leakage.
